To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

i) the stability of protein protein complexes is not determined by electrostatics alone, ii) the stability of a protein protein complex is determined by the hydrophobicity of the interface, and iii) protein disorder at the interface of the complexes can lead to destabilization.
the presence of favorable electrostatics is not a prerequisite for protein protein complex formation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the computational design of protein interfaces and the role of protein flexibility in binding.
the computational design of protein protein interfaces and the factors that contribute to their stability and binding affinity.
the computational design of protein interfaces, and the structural and energetic determinants of protein protein binding.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
protein protein binding is a complex process and the stability and affinity of protein protein complexes are dictated by a number of factors.
the structural and energetic properties of the binding epitope, the receptor, and the interface are all critical for the formation of stable protein protein complexes.
a designer protein protein complex is more likely to be stable if it has more favorable non polar interactions and less favorable entropy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
protein protein binding is an entropically unfavorable process and that the hydrophobic effect is the dominant driving force for protein protein binding.
the stability of the interface between proteins is governed by the interplay of non polar effects and favorable electrostatics, and is opposed by entropy.

protein interfaces are more than just a set of hot spot residues and that the stability and binding affinity of a protein complex is a result of a complex interplay of structural, energetic and thermodynamic factors.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a number of factors including favorable electrostatic interactions, favorable hydrophobic effects and favorable contacts between hot spots and surrounding residues contribute to the stability of protein protein complexes.
the binding epitope alone does not determine the stability of a protein complex, and the role of the receptor is critical.
the design of a stable protein protein complex is more complex and subtle than previously thought.
